outcome: Segmentation policy is derived from how workloads actually behave, enforced next to each workload, with compensating rules covering gaps until patched.
overview: Segmentation projects usually stall at the same place: nobody is willing to enforce a policy because nobody is certain what will break. Cisco Hypershield uses kernel-level observation to build the policy from what workloads actually do, then enforces it close to the workload rather than at a network chokepoint. The interesting property is the ability to compensate for a vulnerability at the workload boundary while a patch is scheduled — which is useful precisely because patching windows are the constraint that segmentation projects run into.

benefits.text: Segmentation policy is derived from observed workload behaviour rather than from a design nobody trusts
benefits.limits: Basis: hypothesis. Observation captures what happened during the window; a quarterly job or a failover path that did not run will not appear and must be sought explicitly

benefits.text: Enforcement sits close to the workload, so it applies wherever the workload runs
benefits.limits: Basis: hypothesis. Kernel-level enforcement constrains supported operating system and kernel versions, which must be checked against the estate before scoping

benefits.text: A vulnerability can be compensated for at the workload boundary while a patch is scheduled
benefits.limits: Basis: hypothesis. Compensation is a delay mechanism; treating it as a substitute for patching is how a temporary control becomes a permanent exposure

residency: Management is cloud-delivered while enforcement runs on the workload; policy and telemetry metadata leave the estate and the tenant region is recorded at design

notFor.situation: An estate already segmented with an agent-based platform in enforcement
notFor.why: Two enforcement agents on one workload contend, and attribution of a connectivity failure becomes expensive

notFor.situation: An estate on operating system versions outside the supported kernel matrix
notFor.why: Kernel-level enforcement has hard prerequisites that no amount of design will work around

scope:
Model: Redington solutions engineering with an accredited Cisco security implementation partner · Duration: 10–14 weeks including an observation window that covers a full business cycle
Support model: Vendor subscription support; Redington coordinates the vendor case. A quarterly capability review is recommended given the pace of change in this product.
1) Check — supported kernel and operating system matrix against the estate, exclusions listed
2) Observe — workload communication recorded across a full business cycle, periodic jobs sought explicitly
3) Derive and review — policy proposed, reviewed and accepted by a named reviewer
4) Enforce and hand over — enforcement on the first groups, compensating-control practice established, operations handed over
deliverables: Every enforced policy retains the observation data that justified it
Known periodic workload behaviours are demonstrably present in the observation set before enforcement
Every compensating rule carries a patch date and expires with it
effort: 10–14 weeks including an observation window that covers a full business cycle
